title: Contemplate, and Thoughts Immediately Rest
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: “Contemplate, and thoughts immediately rest” — what does this mean?

inline.s: Question: “Contemplate, and thoughts immediately rest” — what does this mean?

Answer: It means that when one turns back to observe deluded thoughts, the deluded thoughts cease of themselves. Here “rest” means to come to a stop. This line comes from Master Tanxu’s Recollections of Shadows and Dust, and it is a very vivid description of the initial work of observing the mind. It is quoted below:

“During the Chan seven-day retreat, our meditation was examined once every four days. When going for the examination, one had to wear the long robe and the robe-and-cloth, and carry the sitting cloth, then go to the head-monk or to the abbot; snap! snap! snap! three snaps of the fingers, and one was invited into the room, where one made the customary bow, spread out the sitting cloth, paid homage to the Buddha three times, knelt upright, and joined the palms. When questioned, one had to tell the truth about one’s insight and attainment. At this time some would speak of ‘emptiness’ and some of ‘existence,’ each saying something different. In the end the head-monk would always give a few whacks with the incense board and scold them roundly: ‘You good-for-nothing! Go back and investigate properly!’ And so, in turn, one after another, everyone went for examination. Those whose work was not yet fitting or in accord with the Dharma all had to receive the incense board. Once, I went to Master Dixian to seek instruction. After I had finished the prostrations, the old master first asked: ‘How is your practice going?’ ‘Nothing special!’ I said: ‘When I first sat in meditation, deluded thoughts surged up directly, like waves in the ocean, one wave chasing the next and the next chasing the one before, without end; try as I might to suppress them, I could not, and my mind was very anxious. Later, instead of suppressing them, I used the power of contemplation to observe them,
watching to see just where the deluded thoughts arose from

, and with this single observation the deluded thoughts vanished; when they vanished and rose again, I observed them again. After a long time, gradually the deluded thoughts no longer arose, and my mind became very tranquil and natural.’ ‘Hmm—’ Master Dixian said: ‘You have truly learned how to apply the work! Go back and cultivate like this, and from now on you need not come again.’

I saw that when others went to be examined on their practice, they always had to receive a few scoldings and a few whacks of the incense board before returning. This time, when I went to Master Dixian and described my method of practice, I was neither scolded nor struck with the incense board, and came straight back. Though I said nothing of it aloud, I was naturally very happy in my heart! From then on I used this
method of observing deluded thoughts

in my cultivation. Once, while sitting the late second-incense period, I felt that I had only just crossed my legs when the sitting ended; later a neighbor in the hall told me that one full incense period had long since passed. In that one incense period, although I felt that not much time had passed, my body and mind felt tranquil and at ease, very much in accord with the Dharma, with an indescribable enjoyment. Unconsciously, two lines welled up from the ground of my nature, namely:
‘Contemplate, and thoughts immediately rest; awaken to the false, and the false all becomes true.’
At first I did not dare to regard these two lines as correct, but later I went to ask Master Dixian, and Master Dixian gave them his confirmation.”
Question: “Awaken to the false, and the false all becomes true” — what does this mean?

Answer: “Awaken to the false, and the false all becomes true” means: when one’s awareness illuminates the state of the deluded mind, the deluded mind transforms into the state of the true mind. Master Tanxu continued:
Originally, the practice of the Tiantai school is to observe the sixth consciousness
(the mental consciousness)
— the single thought presently before the mind. When first observing, do not be afraid of deluded thoughts arising, and do not grow anxious in the heart, wanting to get rid of
(eliminate)

the deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts do arise, you may go looking for the deluded thought, observe the deluded thought, as if catching a thief, and see just where the deluded thought comes from and where it goes to. Because the false arises from the true: without the false there is no true, and without the true there is no false. To seek the true, one must seek it within the false. As it is said: ‘Affliction is bodhi; birth and death are nirvāṇa.’ Although at first it is the deluded mind, observe it over and over, and it becomes the true mind. Otherwise, where would there be a separate true mind? Know that the true mind does not leave the deluded mind, and the deluded mind does not leave the true mind. The true and the false are non-dual yet dual, dual yet non-dual. Therefore those who are just beginning to apply the work should not be afraid of deluded thoughts; when deluded thoughts arise, use the wisdom that can observe to observe them, and the deluded thoughts will come to rest. At the same time, be aware that this deluded mind is itself the true mind — there is no other true mind apart from the deluded mind.”

[True and false are non-dual yet dual, dual yet non-dual] This means that the deluded mind and the true mind are one essence with two states. “Dual” refers to the two states (the deluded mind and the true mind are two different states); “non-dual” refers to their being one in essence (the deluded mind and the true mind are the same mind-essence). [One essence, two states] The same mind-essence (self-nature): when it is in the state of having thoughts, it is called the deluded mind; when it is in the state of no-thought, it is called the true mind.

[True mind, deluded mind] The functioning of self-nature is called mind. As it is said, “nature is the essence, mind is the function”: self-nature is the essence of the mind, and mind is the function of self-nature. The mind has two states. First, the fundamental mind, the original state of the mind — spiritually luminous, penetrating and clear, standing alone and independent. Second, the cognitive mind. The cognitive mind is also called the mind of conditioned reflection — the mind that arises by clinging to the six sense-objects, which is what the Buddha in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment called “the conditioned shadows of the six sense-objects.” Its characteristic is discrimination and calculation, attraction and aversion, grasping and rejecting. The arising of thoughts, seeing and hearing, perceiving and knowing (here “knowing” is discriminative knowing) — all of these are the cognitive mind at work. The fundamental mind is also called the true mind (here “true” means original), and the cognitive mind is also called the deluded mind (here “deluded” means falsely stirred — disorder). The true mind is awakening; the deluded mind is confusion. Cultivation is the stilling of the false to reveal the true, as it is said: “If the wild mind does not cease, the ceasing itself is bodhi.” (See in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
